newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate campaign fund probe off to bumpy start.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate campaign fund probe off to bumpy start.

text.p: The Senate committee that will probe campaign finance abuses got off to a rocky start on Wednesday when its chairman failed to win quick acceptance of a $6.5 million budget to hire 80 new investigators and staff.

Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Fred Thompson had hoped the 16-member panel would approve the budget smoothly but he ran into Democratic objections about the size of the budget and scope of the investigation.

The Tennessee Republican asked the committee to approve a routine budget of $4.6 million for its legislative activities this year and an additional $6.5 million for investigating controversial donations during the 1996 presidential election.
After much wrangling among Democrats and Republicans, Thompson put off a vote on the budget until Thursday so staffs could try to work out rules and areas for investigation.

While Thompson repeatedly said the probe would not necessarily be confined to the 1996 election, Democrats led by Sen. John Glenn of Ohio demanded that the committee put in writing that the inquiry be expanded beyond presidential campaign financing to include congressional campaigns as well.

Republicans outnumber Democrats on the committee 9-7 and Thompson could have rammed the budget through but he said he did not want to start the investigation "on a divisive note." Once the committee approves its budget, it must go through the Senate Rules Committee and the Senate itself.

The committee bickered for more than two hours over whether the investigation would be conducted in a bipartisan manner, which both parties said they wanted, and over what would be covered by the probe.

Republican Sen. Ted Stevens of Alaska said, "we're talking about another Watergate," referring to the investigation of wrongdoing during the administration of President Richard Nixon that led to his resignation in 1974.

Glenn, joined by Pennsylvania Republican Arlen Specter, took issue with characterisations of the probe as another Watergate. Glenn raised questions about the $6.5 million budget, telling reporters he knew of nothing to justify a comparison of the campaign finance matter to Watergate.
He expressed confidence that differences on the budget and the scope of the inquiry could be patched up.

By comparison, the select Senate Watergate investigating committee had a budget of about $2 million in 1973 and 1974, which would translate to about $6.8 million in 1996 dollars, according to the Congressional Research Service.

The Senate investigation is only one of many inquiries into improper or illegal finance practices that became an issue in the 1996 presidental election, centred on large contributions to Democrats from Asian Americans and people with ties to foreign businesses.

The FBI has assigned a 25-agent task force to look into economic and national security aspects of campaign financing. In addition, there are House inquiries and the Federal Election Commission is looking into campaign finance problems.
